strengths: Identifies a novel and important safety-critical vulnerability (3D Mirage) affecting multiple SOTA depth estimation architectures, highly relevant for autonomous driving deployment
Creates a valuable benchmark dataset (3D-Mirage) with 1,872 carefully annotated real-world images covering diverse hallucination scenarios (street art, murals, perspective paintings)
Proposes well-motivated problem-specific metrics (DCS for structural deviation, CCS for contextual instability) that directly target the failure mode rather than generic accuracy measures
Demonstrates strong empirical results: 93.5% reduction in geometric hallucinations and 86% reduction in contextual instability while preserving general knowledge (R²≈93%)
Provides comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, domain analysis (indoor/outdoor), extended training analysis, and detailed failure mode characterization
Proposes a practical, parameter-efficient solution using LoRA adapters (~0.7% additional parameters) that is deployable and effective
Well-written paper with clear presentation and effective visualizations (heatmaps, comparisons) that clearly illustrate both the problem and solution
weaknesses: Limited architectural generalization: Primary solution validated on DAv2-L with less comprehensive results on other models; applicability to future transformer-based or fundamentally different architectures unclear

Narrow problem scope: Focuses specifically on planar surface illusions; does not address other hallucination types (reflections, transparent surfaces, lighting-induced artifacts) limiting broader impact

Metric validation incomplete: DCS and CCS lack independent validation against human judgment; metric design choices (99th percentile) lack justification; problem-specific metrics may not transfer to other hallucination types

Training data curation bias: 4:1 positive/negative sample ratio chosen empirically without ablation; manual dataset curation may not represent all real-world hallucination patterns; impact of ratio vs. loss functions unknown

Loss function design under-justified: Specific HKR loss formulation (Eq. 9) lacks theoretical justification; choice of second-order smoothness in Eq. 10 unexplained; no ablation on loss term weights (σ₁-σ₅)

Incomplete failure analysis: While Figure G shows failures, characterization of remaining failure modes is limited; unclear if benchmark becomes too easy post-mitigation or if method truly solves the problem
No computational cost analysis: Training overhead and memory requirements not reported; inference cost not explicitly confirmed despite LoRA efficiency claims

Limited alternative approach comparison: No comparison with other potential mitigation strategies (explicit geometry constraints, global context modeling, uncertainty estimation, adversarial training); justification for why distillation is superior absent

Knowledge preservation trade-offs underexplored: While R² remains high, which specific knowledge is preserved vs. lost is unclear; extended training degradation (Table A) suggests possible fundamental limitations

Shallow root cause analysis: Paper identifies over-reliance on global semantic priors but doesn't explain why; unclear if problem is fundamental to scale-based learning or addressable through better training data

Generalization to unseen illusions not tested: No evaluation on out-of-distribution hallucination types; cross-domain generalization to novel illusion patterns unknown; unclear if method generalizes or memorizes benchmark
Minimal societal impact discussion: Limited guidance on when corrected predictions can be trusted in safety-critical systems; no analysis of potential failure consequences for autonomous driving

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem identification: The 3D-Mirage failure mode is a genuine safety concern for autonomous driving, demonstrated systematically across multiple SOTA models
Valuable benchmark contribution: The 3D-Mirage dataset with 1,872 annotated images and precise planar region masks provides a useful resource for the community
Thoughtfully designed metrics: DCS and CCS metrics specifically capture failure modes (spurious non-planarity and contextual instability) rather than relying on generic pixel-level errors
Comprehensive empirical analysis: Detailed breakdowns of failure modes including Laplacian response visualizations, domain specialization effects, and architectural comparisons
Parameter-efficient mitigation: The Grounded Self-Distillation method achieves substantial improvements (93.5% DCS reduction, 86% CCS reduction) with minimal trainable parameters (0.7% via LoRA)
Thorough experimental validation: Good ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of each component
weaknesses: Severely limited problem scope: Focuses narrowly on planar surfaces with optical illusions (street art); unclear how findings generalize to other hallucination modes or depth anomalies beyond this specific scenario

Inadequate practical deployment solution: Requires manual ROI annotations with geometric knowledge during training; no mechanism for automatic illusion detection in real-world scenarios, severely limiting applicability

Weak theoretical understanding: The paper diagnoses what happens but provides limited insight into why models hallucinate; explanations remain phenomenological without deeper analysis of learned representations or architectural causes

Insufficient end-to-end validation: No demonstration that fixing 3D-Mirage improves downstream autonomous driving tasks (e.g., object detection, safety metrics); practical impact for real systems unclear

Incremental methodology: Grounded Self-Distillation is essentially weighted knowledge distillation with LoRA—not particularly novel; simpler alternatives (confidence calibration, uncertainty estimation) not explored
Metric-centric improvements: Improvements are most pronounced on custom metrics (DCS/CCS); standard metric improvements are modest (e.g., Table 1 shows relatively small absolute differences)
Generalization not demonstrated: No evidence that adapters trained on benchmark illusions generalize to unseen illusion patterns; potential overfitting to dataset-specific artifacts
Missing reproducibility details: Inter-annotator agreement not reported, exact train/test splits unspecified, no explicit code/data release confirmation despite reproducibility claims

Questionable evaluation design: Evaluates hallucination intensity without validating whether humans perceive corrected depth as actually more accurate; unclear if CCS correlates with real-world safety issues

Limited scope to safety-critical but niche failure mode: While the problem is real, it addresses one specific phenomenon among many potential depth estimation failures; unclear if this is the most impactful issue to solve

strengths: Identifies and systematically characterizes an important, previously under-explored failure mode (3D Mirage) affecting all SOTA depth estimation models, with clear practical implications for safety-critical applications
Introduces a carefully designed 3D-Mirage benchmark with 1,872 precisely annotated real-world images and a rigorous three-stage collection pipeline specifically targeting the hallucination problem

Proposes purpose-built evaluation metrics (DCS and CCS) tailored to measure hallucination intensity and contextual instability, which are more meaningful than standard depth metrics for this failure mode
Comprehensive experimental validation across 10+ architectures with thorough ablation studies demonstrating systematic vulnerability and validating each component of the proposed solution

Practical Grounded Self-Distillation method is parameter-efficient (4M parameters, <0.7% of backbone) achieving 93% hallucination reduction while maintaining reasonable general performance (89.73% R²)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology; authors indicate commitment to releasing code and benchmark to enable future research
Demonstrates that hallucination is a systemic issue across different model architectures and training paradigms, suggesting this is a fundamental limitation rather than isolated to specific models
weaknesses: Limited scope of applicability: focus is primarily on planar surfaces misperceived as non-planar in driving scenarios with street art and optical illusions; generalization to other domains and non-planar hallucinations unclear

Trade-off between hallucination removal and general knowledge preservation not thoroughly analyzed; R² drops from 100% (baseline) to 89.73% (full method) and the Pareto frontier between these objectives deserves deeper exploration

Novel metrics (DCS, CCS) lack human evaluation validation; no user studies confirming that reducing these metrics correlates with perceptually meaningful improvements or safety benefits in downstream tasks
Limited baseline comparisons with alternative hallucination mitigation strategies (ensemble methods, uncertainty quantification, post-processing); method is only compared against the teacher baseline
Dataset scale (1,872 images) is relatively small for training robust models; no inter-rater agreement analysis for manual mask annotations, and unclear whether annotation quality is sufficient
Design choices appear somewhat arbitrary without sufficient justification: context-restricted crop ratio (40%) lacks ablation, gating network architecture and temperature parameters not explained
Incomplete failure case analysis: Figure O shows some limitations but analysis is brief; unclear performance on complex multi-pattern scenes or textured surfaces without clear geometric ambiguity
Missing computational analysis: no discussion of inference time overhead or memory requirements relative to baseline, which is important for real-world deployment
The solution is specifically tailored to planar-surface hallucinations; generalization to other hallucination types (phantom objects, texture confusions) is unexplored
